title: Gravity: What Keeps Us on the Ground
summary: How gravity pulls objects together, keeps us on the ground, sets our weight, holds the Moon and planets in orbit, and causes tides.
poll: Gravity is the most important force in our everyday lives.

versions.title: Gravity Pulls Down
versions.text:
Drop a ball. It falls down. Why? A pull makes it fall. The pull is called gravity.

Gravity is a force. A force is a push or a pull. Gravity is a pull.

All things pull on all things. Big things pull hard. Earth is very big. So it pulls us down. That is why we stay on the ground. That is why a ball comes back down.

Your weight is how hard Earth pulls on you.

The Moon is small. It pulls less. On the Moon, you would weigh much less. You could jump very high!

The Moon goes round and round Earth. Its path is called an orbit. Gravity keeps it there. Earth has an orbit, too. It goes round the Sun.

The Moon pulls on the sea, too. The sea goes up and down each day. This is the tide.

Long ago, a man named Isaac Newton saw that one pull drops an apple and holds the Moon. That pull is gravity.

versions.title: Gravity Pulls Down
versions.text:
Drop a ball and watch it. It falls to the ground. It does not float up. A pull makes it fall. This pull is called gravity.

Gravity is a force. A force is a push or a pull. Gravity is always a pull.

All things pull on all other things. Big things pull the most. Earth is very, very big. So it pulls us down toward its middle. That is why we stay on the ground. That is why a ball you kick comes back down.

Your weight tells how hard Earth pulls on you.

The Moon is much smaller than Earth. Its pull is weaker. On the Moon, you would weigh much less. You could jump very high!

The Moon moves round and round Earth. Its path is called an orbit. Gravity holds the Moon in its orbit. Earth has an orbit, too. It goes round the Sun.

The Moon pulls on the sea. The sea rises and falls each day. This is called the tide.

Long ago, a man named Isaac Newton had a big idea. He said the pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon. That pull is gravity.

versions.title: Gravity: The Pull That Holds Us
versions.text:
Throw a ball up into the air. It goes up for a bit. Then it comes back down. Something pulls it to the ground. That pull is called gravity.

Gravity is a force. A force is a push or a pull that can move things. Gravity is always a pull.

Every object pulls on every other object. Big things pull the hardest. Our planet Earth is huge, so its pull is strong. It pulls all things toward its center. That is why we stay on the ground. It is why we do not float away.

Your weight tells how hard Earth pulls on you.

The Moon is much smaller than Earth. Its gravity is weaker. On the Moon, you would weigh much less. Astronauts on the Moon could bounce and jump high.

The Moon moves around Earth on a path. The path is called an orbit. Gravity keeps the Moon from flying off into space. In the same way, Earth moves in an orbit around the Sun.

The Moon's pull tugs on the seas, too. The water rises and falls on the shore each day. These changes are called tides.

Long ago, a scientist named Isaac Newton explained gravity. He saw that the pull that drops an apple also keeps the Moon in its orbit.

versions.title: Gravity: The Pull That Holds Us
versions.text:
Kick a football high into the air, and it always comes back down. It never keeps rising into the sky. A pull you cannot see brings it back to the ground. Scientists call this pull gravity.

Gravity is a force. A force is any push or pull that can make a thing move, stop, or turn. Gravity is always a pull, never a push.

Every object pulls on every other object. The bigger and heavier a thing is, the stronger its pull. Earth is huge, so its gravity is strong. It pulls all things toward its center. That is why we stay on the ground and do not float away.

Your weight tells how hard Earth's gravity pulls on you.

The Moon is much smaller than Earth, so its gravity is weaker. On the Moon, you would weigh only about one sixth of what you weigh at home. Astronauts who walked there could bounce and leap with ease.

The Moon moves around Earth on a curved path called an orbit. Gravity keeps it from drifting off into space. In the same way, Earth moves in an orbit around the Sun.

The Moon's gravity also tugs on the seas. The water rises and falls along the shore each day. These changes are called tides.

More than three hundred years ago, a scientist named Isaac Newton explained gravity. He saw that the same pull that drops an apple also keeps the Moon in its orbit.

versions.title: Gravity: What Keeps Us on the Ground
versions.text:
Kick a football as high as you can, and it always falls back to the ground. Jump off a step, and you land a moment later. Each time, the same force is at work, and that force is gravity.

Gravity is a pull. Every object that has mass pulls on, or attracts, every other object. Mass is the amount of matter, or stuff, in something. The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull. Distance matters too, because the farther apart two objects are, the weaker the pull between them.

Earth has a huge mass, so its gravity is strong. It pulls everything toward its center. That is why people all around the world feel that "down" is under their feet.

Your mass stays the same wherever you go, but your weight can change. Weight is how hard gravity pulls on your mass. The Moon has much less mass than Earth, so on the Moon you would weigh only about one sixth as much.

Gravity also keeps the Moon in its orbit. The Moon is moving very fast, and without gravity it would fly off in a straight line. Earth's pull bends its path into a loop around our planet. In the same way, the Sun's gravity keeps Earth in its orbit.

The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans. This pull helps cause the tides, the daily rise and fall of the sea.

In 1971, an astronaut did a famous experiment on the Moon. He dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time, and because the Moon has no air to slow the feather, both landed together.

Isaac Newton first explained gravity more than three hundred years ago, when he saw that the pull that makes an apple fall also holds the Moon in its orbit.

versions.text:

Mass is the amount of matter, or material, that something contains. The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull. Distance matters as well, because the farther apart two objects are, the weaker the attraction between them becomes.

Because Earth has an enormous mass, its gravity is powerful. It pulls everything toward the center of the planet, which is why people everywhere feel that "down" is beneath their feet, even on the opposite side of the world.

Your mass stays the same wherever you travel, but your weight can change. Weight is a measure of how strongly gravity pulls on your mass. The Moon has far less mass than Earth, so an astronaut standing on the Moon weighs only about one sixth as much as on Earth.

In the same way, the Sun's gravity keeps Earth moving in its yearly orbit.

The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans as well, and this pull helps produce the tides, the regular rise and fall of sea level along the coast.

versions.title: Gravity: The Force That Holds Our World Together
versions.text:
Kick a football as high as you can, and it will inevitably return to the ground. Leap from a step, and you land a fraction of a second later. In both situations the same invisible force is responsible, and scientists call it gravity.

Gravity is an attraction that operates across space. Every object that possesses mass attracts every other object, whether it is a grain of sand or an entire planet. Mass is the amount of matter that something contains, and the more mass an object has, the stronger its gravitational pull. Distance is equally important, because the attraction between two objects grows weaker as they move farther apart.

Because Earth has an enormous mass, its gravity is powerful. It draws everything toward the center of the planet, which explains why people everywhere experience "down" as the direction beneath their feet, even on the opposite side of the globe.

Your mass remains the same wherever you travel, but your weight can change. Weight is a measurement of how strongly gravity pulls on your mass. Since the Moon has considerably less mass than Earth, an astronaut standing on its surface weighs only about one sixth as much as at home.

Gravity also explains why the Moon remains in its orbit. The Moon is traveling rapidly, and without gravity it would continue away in a straight line. Earth's attraction continually bends that path into a loop around our planet. Similarly, the Sun's gravity keeps Earth moving along its yearly orbit.

The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans as well, and this pull helps produce the tides, the regular rise and fall of sea level along coastlines.

In 1971, an astronaut conducted a famous experiment on the Moon. He released a hammer and a feather at precisely the same instant. Since the Moon has no air to slow the feather, both objects landed simultaneously, demonstrating that gravity makes all objects fall at the same rate when air is absent.

Isaac Newton first described gravity mathematically more than three hundred years ago. He recognized that the force causing an apple to fall is identical to the force holding the Moon in its orbit.

versions.title: Gravity: The Force That Holds Our World Together
versions.text:
Kick a football as high as you can, and it will inevitably return to the ground. Leap from a step, and you land a fraction of a second later. In both situations the same invisible force is responsible, and scientists call it gravity.

More than three hundred years ago, in 1687, the English scientist Isaac Newton published a theory explaining this force. According to a well-known story, he was thinking about a falling apple when he wondered whether the pull that brought the apple down might also reach as far as the Moon. His conclusion was that every object with mass exerts an attraction on every other object, from a grain of sand to an entire planet.

Mass is the amount of matter an object contains, and Newton showed that the attraction depends on two factors: objects with greater mass pull more strongly, and the pull weakens rapidly as the distance between objects increases.

Because Earth has an enormous mass, its gravity is powerful. It draws everything toward the center of the planet, which explains why people everywhere experience "down" as the direction beneath their feet, even on the opposite side of the globe.

Your mass remains constant wherever you travel, but your weight can change, because weight is a measurement of how strongly gravity pulls on your mass. Since the Moon has considerably less mass than Earth, an astronaut on its surface weighs only about one sixth as much as at home.

Gravity also explains orbits. The Moon travels rapidly, and without gravity it would continue away in a straight line, but Earth's attraction continually bends its path into a loop, while the Sun's gravity holds Earth in its yearly orbit in the same way. Astronauts aboard a space station float not because gravity has vanished but because they and their station are constantly falling around Earth together.

The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans, and this pull helps produce the tides, the regular rise and fall of sea level along coastlines.

In 1971, an astronaut tested a famous prediction on the Moon. He released a hammer and a feather at the same instant. Because the Moon has almost no air, its surface is close to a vacuum, so nothing slowed the feather, and both objects landed simultaneously. The demonstration proved that, without air resistance, gravity makes all objects fall at the same rate.

versions.title: Gravity: The Invisible Force That Shapes the Universe
versions.text:

In 1687, the English mathematician and scientist Isaac Newton published a theory explaining this force. Mass is the quantity of matter an object contains, and Newton demonstrated that gravitational attraction depends on two factors. Objects with greater mass exert a stronger pull, whereas the attraction diminishes rapidly as the distance separating two objects increases.

Because Earth possesses an enormous mass, its gravity is considerable, drawing everything toward the center of the planet; consequently, people everywhere experience "down" as the direction beneath their feet, even on the opposite side of the globe.

The Moon's gravity additionally tugs on Earth's oceans, and this attraction helps generate the tides, the regular rise and fall of sea level along coastlines.

In 1971, an astronaut tested a celebrated prediction on the lunar surface by releasing a hammer and a feather at the same instant. keyWords.definition: the pull that makes things fall down to the ground
keyWords.example: When I let go of my pen, gravity made it drop to the floor.

keyWords.definition: a push or a pull that can make something move
keyWords.example: It took a lot of force to open the heavy door.

keyWords.definition: how heavy something is; how hard Earth pulls on it
keyWords.example: The nurse checked my weight on a scale.

keyWords.definition: the path one thing takes as it goes around and around another thing
keyWords.example: A satellite moves in an orbit high above Earth.

keyWords.definition: the rise and fall of the sea each day
keyWords.example: We built our sand castle far from the water before the tide came in.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to throw and kick a ball very high into the sky
How gravity pulls on things and holds them in place
Why the Moon looks bigger on some nights than others
How to grow apples on a farm
questions.why: The whole article explains gravity: how it pulls things down, sets our weight, holds the Moon in orbit, and moves the sea.

wrong.A: A ball is used as an example, but the article is not about throwing.
wrong.C: The article says the Moon is smaller than Earth, not bigger.
wrong.D: An apple is part of the Newton story, but the article is not about farming.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is your weight?
options: How tall you are
How fast you can run in a race at school
How old you are
How hard Earth pulls on you
questions.why: The article says your weight tells how hard Earth pulls on you.

wrong.A: Height is not the same as weight.
wrong.B: The article does not connect weight to running.
wrong.C: Age has nothing to do with weight in the article.

questions.stem: What does the Moon's pull do to the sea?
options: It makes the water rise and fall each day
It makes the water turn very cold in the winter
It makes the sea dry up
It makes big fish swim faster near the shore
questions.why: The article says the Moon pulls on the sea, and the water rises and falls. These changes are the tides.

wrong.B: The article does not say the Moon changes how cold the water is.
wrong.C: The sea does not dry up; it rises and falls.
wrong.D: Fish are not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: The article says the Moon goes around Earth in an orbit. What is an orbit?
options: A strong pull
A kind of rock on the Moon
A path around something
A big wave in the sea
questions.why: The article calls the Moon's path around Earth an orbit.

wrong.A: A strong pull is gravity, not an orbit.
wrong.B: An orbit is not a rock.
wrong.D: A rise of the sea is a tide, not an orbit.

questions.stem: Why would you weigh less on the Moon?
options: Because there is no ground on the Moon
Because you would be wearing a space suit
Because the Moon is smaller and its pull is weaker
Because the Moon is very cold and has no water at all
questions.why: The article says the Moon is smaller than Earth, so it pulls less, and you would weigh less there.

wrong.A: There is ground on the Moon; astronauts walked on it.
wrong.B: A space suit would add weight, not take it away.
wrong.D: Cold is not the reason the article gives.

questions.stem: Which of these would have the strongest pull?
options: The Sun
A football
A small rock
A school bus
questions.why: The article says big things pull the hardest. The Sun is by far the biggest thing in the list, and it is strong enough to hold Earth in its orbit.

wrong.B: A football is small, so its pull is tiny.
wrong.C: A small rock has very little pull.
wrong.D: A bus is big for a car, but it is tiny next to the Sun.

questions.stem: A boy drops his pencil. What can you tell from the article?
options: The pencil will float in the air
The pencil will fall because the Moon pulls it
The pencil will go up first and then float slowly away
The pencil will fall because Earth pulls it down
questions.why: The article says Earth is big and pulls things down, so a dropped pencil falls to the ground.

wrong.A: Things do not float on Earth because gravity pulls them down.
wrong.B: Earth's pull, not the Moon's, makes things fall to the ground.
wrong.C: A dropped pencil has nothing pushing it up.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about Isaac Newton?
options: To show that he liked to sit under apple trees and eat apples
To tell who saw that the same pull drops an apple and holds the Moon
To explain how a child can study hard and become a scientist
To show that people long ago could not see the Moon
questions.why: The author tells about Newton because he saw that one pull, gravity, drops an apple and also holds the Moon.

wrong.A: The apple is part of his idea, not about what he liked to eat.
wrong.C: The article does not explain how to become a scientist.
wrong.D: The article does not say people could not see the Moon.

A magnet can attract paper clips from across the table.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Astronauts enjoy jumping and bouncing on the Moon because it is fun.
Isaac Newton was the first person to see an apple fall.
Gravity is a pull between objects with mass that explains weight, orbits, tides, and falling.
The Moon has no air, so feathers and hammers cannot be used there by astronauts.
questions.why: Each part of the article shows a different job that gravity does: making things fall, setting weight, holding orbits, and causing tides.

wrong.B: The article says Newton explained gravity, not that he was the first to see an apple fall.
wrong.D: The feather was brought to the Moon for an experiment; this is not the main idea.

questions.stem: What is mass, according to the article?
options: The amount of matter in something
How fast something falls
How hard gravity pulls on something
The path something takes around a planet
questions.why: The article defines mass as the amount of matter, or stuff, in something.

wrong.B: Falling speed is not how the article defines mass.
wrong.C: How hard gravity pulls is weight, not mass.
wrong.D: A path around a planet is an orbit.

questions.stem: What happened in the experiment on the Moon in 1971?
options: The feather floated slowly away into space and was lost
The hammer landed first because it was much heavier
The astronaut could not lift the hammer
The hammer and the feather landed at the same time
questions.why: The article says the astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather together, and both landed together.

wrong.A: The feather fell; it did not float away.
wrong.B: The hammer did not land first; they landed together.
wrong.C: The article does not say he could not lift the hammer.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: "Every object that has mass attracts every other object." What does attracts mean?
options: Pushes away
Pulls toward itself
Spins around
Breaks apart
questions.why: Gravity is described as a pull, so attracts means pulls toward itself.

wrong.A: Gravity is always a pull, not a push.
wrong.C: Spinning is not part of the meaning.
wrong.D: Nothing breaks apart in the sentence.

questions.stem: Why did the feather fall as fast as the hammer on the Moon?
options: The feather was made of a heavy metal instead of real feathers
The astronaut threw the feather harder
The Moon has no air to slow the feather down
The Moon's gravity is stronger than Earth's
questions.why: The article explains that the Moon has no air, so nothing slowed the feather, and both landed together.

wrong.A: The feather was a normal feather, not metal.
wrong.B: He dropped both at the same time; he did not throw them.
wrong.D: The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, not stronger.

questions.stem: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. What happens to her mass and her weight?
options: Her mass stays the same, but her weight becomes less
Her mass and weight both become less
Her mass becomes less, but her weight stays the same
Her mass and weight both stay the same
questions.why: The article says mass stays the same wherever you go, but weight changes. On the Moon, she weighs about one sixth as much.

wrong.B: Mass does not change when you travel.
wrong.C: This is the reverse of what the article explains.
wrong.D: Her weight does change because the Moon's pull is weaker.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if Earth's gravity suddenly stopped pulling on the Moon?
options: The Moon would crash into Earth
The Moon would stop moving and stay still
The Moon would orbit the Sun faster than Earth
The Moon would move away in a straight line
questions.why: The article says that without gravity, the fast-moving Moon would fly off in a straight line.

wrong.B: The article says the Moon is moving very fast, so it would keep moving.
wrong.C: The article does not suggest this.

questions.stem: How does the author explain the difference between mass and weight?
options: By telling a story about Newton and the apple that fell from a tree
By comparing them and giving the Moon as an example
By listing the steps of the experiment done on the Moon
By describing the tides in the ocean
questions.why: The author compares mass, which stays the same, with weight, which changes, and uses being on the Moon as an example.

wrong.A: The apple story is about how Newton explained gravity, not mass and weight.
wrong.C: The experiment is about falling objects, not mass and weight.
wrong.D: Tides are a different part of the article.

questions.stem: In what year did Isaac Newton publish his theory of gravity?

wrong.A: 1971 is the year of the hammer-and-feather test on the Moon.
wrong.C: The article does not give this date.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do astronauts float aboard a space station?
options: Gravity cannot reach that far from the surface of Earth
The station has its own engines that push them upward
They are constantly falling around Earth with the station
Their mass becomes zero once they leave Earth's air
questions.why: The article says astronauts float not because gravity disappears but because they and the station are continuously falling around Earth.

wrong.A: The article says gravity has not disappeared there.
wrong.B: The article does not mention engines pushing astronauts.
wrong.D: The article says mass stays constant wherever you travel.

questions.stem: The article says the Moon's surface is nearly a vacuum. What does vacuum mean in this context?
options: A place with almost no air
A place with very strong gravity
A machine that cleans floors
A deep hole in the ground
questions.why: The article connects vacuum to the Moon having almost no atmosphere, so it means a place with almost no air.

wrong.B: The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, and vacuum is about air, not gravity.
wrong.C: That is a different meaning of the word, not the meaning in this article.
wrong.D: The word describes a lack of air, not a hole.

questions.stem: What caused the hammer and the feather to land at the same moment on the Moon?
options: The astronaut threw the feather downward
There was almost no air to slow the feather
The Moon's gravity pulls harder on light objects
The feather was heavier than it looked

wrong.C: The article says gravity accelerates all objects at the same rate.

questions.stem: Two spacecraft drift farther and farther apart. Based on the article, what happens to the gravitational attraction between them?
options: It stays exactly the same
It becomes stronger
It disappears immediately
It becomes weaker
questions.why: Newton showed that attraction weakens as the distance between objects increases.

wrong.A: The article says distance changes the strength of the pull.
wrong.B: Moving apart weakens the pull rather than strengthening it.
wrong.C: The pull weakens, but the article does not say it vanishes at once.

questions.stem: What does the apple story suggest about Newton's way of thinking?
options: He linked an ordinary event on Earth to the motion of the Moon
He believed that apples and the Moon are made of exactly the same material
He wanted to prove that apples fall faster than other objects
He thought gravity only worked on Earth
questions.why: Newton wondered whether the pull that dropped an apple also reached the Moon, connecting an everyday event to space.

wrong.B: The article says nothing about what the Moon is made of.
wrong.C: The article does not say Newton compared falling speeds.
wrong.D: His idea was the opposite: the same pull reaches the Moon.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the explanation of astronauts floating in a space station?
options: To prove that the space station is much too far from Earth for gravity to reach
To correct the common idea that there is no gravity in space
To explain how astronauts train before a mission
To show that the Moon has no atmosphere
